title: First USGS aftershock forecasts showed no clear magnitude-share error at complete M4 thresholds in a 2019-2026 archive
abstract: We tested whether the magnitude rule can explain early USGS aftershock forecast errors. We reused a fixed operational archive and removed the productivity rate by comparing nested magnitude counts. In 182 non-overlapping first RJ forecast regions with complete one-week windows and stated completeness at M4 or below, 10 of 86 M4+ events were M5+, against 8.6 from the issued rule. The b offset was -0.066 (sequence bootstrap 95% interval -0.243 to +0.355). Only 24 regions supplied events and one supplied 42% of the count. No clear magnitude-share error was found. We also supply a likelihood mixture audit that tests predictable magnitude shares without a Poisson rate assumption, with an exact check and a branching simulation. The simulation gave conservative, not inflated, binomial rejection. This is a null attribution result and a reusable method. It is not independent forecast validation or proof that the magnitude rule is correct. Catalog completeness, secondary triggering, region selection and sparse large events limit inference.

display.caption: Recorded and rule-based M5+ counts given M4+ counts, with sequence bootstrap intervals for a common b offset. The test found no clear magnitude-share error.
